title: Digital transformation of wafer fabrication process: a case of semiconductor manufacturing
summary: Semiconductors are essential for the digital revolution, modern electronics, and global economic growth. However, the growing demand, geopolitical tensions, and supply chain disruptions have accelerated the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technology (DT) in semiconductor manufacturing. To address this gap, we studied five use cases from leading semiconductor manufacturers (Intel, Micron, Sony, Samsung, and SK Hynix). We investigate the application of AI & DT in the semiconductor wafer fabrication process (WFP). We propose a three-layer framework for WFP, consisting of supply chain, manufacturing process, and AI & DT layers, with enabling technologies. The framework incorporates AI & DT into manufacturing process-specific applications, including pattern classification, smart sensors & automation, real-time monitoring, yield prediction, automated material handling systems, predictive maintenance, data integrity, and fault & anomaly detection in semiconductor manufacturing. The implementation of AI & DT in the semiconductor industry has demonstrated significant improvements, including a 35% reduction in quality events (defects) and 25-40% reductions in cycle time. The proposed framework provides a strategy to improve operational efficiency at WFP while overcoming the limitations of the traditional approach. Key research findings highlight the potential impact of leveraging AI & DT in semiconductor WFP.

title: Board sustainability expertise: how shareholder and employee representatives shape supervisory board practice in codetermined German firms
summary: Purpose This paper asks how sustainability expertise is constructed, distributed across shareholder and employee representatives and translated into influence through the governance channels of parity codetermined supervisory boards in German listed corporations, as European sustainability regulation and scrutiny intensify. Design/methodology/approach Thirty-six semi-structured interviews with supervisory board members in parity codetermined listed corporations are analysed abductively through an integrated resource dependence and resource-based perspective. The analysis treats the two theories as jointly explaining how externally oriented resource dependencies and internally grounded capabilities are combined within board processes, tracing how directors construct sustainability expertise, how it is allocated across shareholder and employee benches, and how it becomes consequential through formal and informal governance channels. Findings Sustainability expertise is constructed less as an individual credential than as a collectively developed board capability combining regulatory literacy with operational understanding. Shareholder representatives tend to supply externally oriented regulatory and capital-market knowledge, whereas employee representatives contribute firm- and workforce-grounded implementation insight and longer time horizons. Codetermination thereby broadens the board's resource base but holds these logics in productive tension. Expertise becomes influential only when channelled through committee mandates, agenda-setting authority and informal cross-bench coordination. Boards vary, however, in whether these channels confine expertise to defensible compliance or open it to strategic integration. Research limitations/implications The study is context-specific to large German parity codetermined listed corporations with a mandatory two-tier system. Because strategic sustainability integration unfolds over longer time horizons than a single interview phase can capture, future longitudinal research could trace how the governance channels identified here shape integration over time and across corporate governance regimes. Originality/value This paper opens the boardroom black box by theorising sustainability expertise as a dynamic, collective board capability and by specifying the mechanisms through which it is constructed, reconciled across competing resource logics and mobilised into influence. It shows how codetermination, by combining distinct shareholder and employee resource bases, conditions whose expertise counts and how it is converted into influence.

AI.abstract_translation: 目的 本文提出问题：在欧洲可持续性监管与审查日益强化的背景下，可持续性专长如何在德国上市公司的对等共同决定监事会中形成、如何在股东代表与雇员代表之间分布，并通过治理渠道转化为影响力。设计/方法/路径 本文对来自对等共同决定上市公司的监事会成员的三十六次半结构化访谈，采用整合的资源依赖与资源基础视角进行溯因分析。分析将这两种理论视为共同解释外部导向的资源依赖与内部根植的能力如何在董事会过程中相结合，追踪董事如何建构可持续性专长、其如何在股东方与雇员方之间配置，以及其如何通过正式与非正式治理渠道变得具有实质影响。研究发现 可持续性专长与其说是一种个人资历，不如说是一种集体形成的董事会能力，将监管素养与运营理解相结合。股东代表往往提供外部导向的监管与资本市场知识，而雇员代表则贡献植根于企业与劳动力的实施洞见以及更长的时间视野。共同决定因此拓宽了董事会的资源基础，但同时使这些逻辑处于富有成效的张力之中。专长只有在通过委员会授权、议程设定权以及非正式的跨方协调等渠道被引导时才会产生影响。然而，各董事会在这些渠道是把专长限定于防御性的合规范畴，还是将其开放给战略性整合方面存在差异。研究局限/启示 本研究特定于拥有强制性双层制度的大型德国对等共同决定上市公司。由于战略性可持续性整合所展开的时间跨度长于单一访谈阶段所能捕捉的范围，未来的纵向研究可以追踪此处识别出的治理渠道如何随时间推移以及在不同公司治理体制中塑造这种整合。原创性/价值 本文通过将可持续性专长理论化为一种动态的、集体的董事会能力，并明确指出其被建构、在不同竞争性资源逻辑之间得到协调以及被动员转化为影响力的机制，从而打开了董事会这一黑箱。本文展示了共同决定如何通过结合股东与雇员各自不同的资源基础，界定了谁的专业知识具有分量以及其如何被转化为影响力。

title: Green absorptive capacity and environmental sustainability: unveiling the interplay and moderating roles of blockchain and supply chain finance
summary: Purpose Drawing on dynamic capability theory and the natural resource-based view, this study aims to examine how green absorptive capacity (GAC) enhances environmental sustainability performance (ESP) through financial performance (FP) and operational performance (OP) and how blockchain technology (BCT) and supply chain finance (SCF) strengthen these indirect relationships. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 522 organisations in Egypt and 508 in Jordan. Covariance-based structural equation modelling was used to test the moderated mediation model. Findings The results show that in both Egypt and Jordan, GAC improves ESP indirectly through FP and OP. In Jordan, blockchain technology strengthens the indirect relationship through both financial and operational performance, whereas in Egypt these blockchain effects are not supported. Supply chain finance strengthens the indirect relationship through operational performance in both countries, but not through financial performance. The nested model comparison indicates that whilst the overall model applies to both contexts, BCT and SCF exert varying degrees of influence in Egypt and Jordan. Research limitations/implications The results can support policymakers and organisational stakeholders by showing how digital technologies and green financing mechanisms can be used to strengthen the impact of green knowledge on performance and accelerate progress towards environmental sustainability. Originality/value This study develops and tests an integrated moderated mediation framework explaining how green absorptive capacity enhances environmental sustainability performance through financial and operational performance and how blockchain technology and supply chain finance strengthen these indirect relationships. By comparing Egypt and Jordan, the study extends dynamic capability theory and the natural resource-based view through context-specific evidence from two Arab emerging economies and reveals country-specific differences in the effectiveness of digital and financial enablers.

title: Reversing the role of the customer: the new ‘customer-as-a-supplier’ supply chain principle for the circular context
summary: This paper evaluates the relevance and sufficiency of a suite of six established supply chain principles for uncertainty reduction in circular supply chains, focusing on plastics in the construction sector. Using a structured intervention-based research approach, two trials with industry consortia designed and implemented closed-loop models for mortar tubs and aggregate packaging, incorporating higher recycled content and new reverse logistics arrangements. Findings confirm that original principles remain relevant but insufficient in circular contexts. We propose an additional principle ‘Customer-as-a-Supplier (CaaS)’ to address uncertainties in quality, timing, and volume of returned materials, and the changing role of customers in closed loop supply chains. CaaS emphasises communication, incentives, convenient return logistics, contamination control, and retailer engagement to enable high-quality material recovery. This extends the existing framework and highlights the active, and changing, role of customers. title: Digitalization and Environmental, Social, and Governance Reporting: Evidence from the US Banking Industry
summary: ABSTRACT We examine the relation between digitalization and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) reporting using a sample of listed US banks from 2010 to 2022. Our study is based on a two‐step theoretical framework, building on voluntary disclosure and signaling theory: First, we expect and find technological progress to enhance internal information quality. Second, we examine whether banks pass on this improved information to stakeholders via ESG reports. Our results suggest that banks are more likely to disclose an ESG report as they become more digitalized. Further, we find that digitalization is related to a higher extent and quality of ESG reporting. A difference‐in‐differences test and a mediation analysis corroborate our findings. Cross‐sectional tests indicate an attenuated association between digitalization and ESG reporting for banks with low data privacy and security disclosure. Our findings have practical implications because they highlight the potential of digitalization to improve ESG reporting but also possible drawbacks as digitalization comes along with certain risks.

title: When and How Firms Can Promote Green Innovation for Sustainable Development: A Holistic Examination
summary: Green finance has become a key instrument for addressing environmental degradation and supporting sustainable development. However, existing literature has largely focused on its outcomes, with limited attention to the factors that contribute to its effectiveness. Using an input-oriented perspective, this study examines the roles of green innovation, financial development, and research and development (R&D) in promoting green financing and sustainable development. Empirical data from thirty-nine manufacturing companies in Saudi Arabia covering 2011–2025 are analyzed using partial least squares, generalized method of moments, fixed-effects, and random-effects models. The findings demonstrate that green innovation, financial development, and R&D significantly contribute to the effectiveness of green financing. The transition from conventional product innovation to green finance is found to be less challenging than the development of eco-friendly technological innovations, as environmentally friendly products can generate positive financial returns. The study provides policy insights for promoting sustainable industrial growth.

title: THE PERIPHERAL PLACE OF SUSTAINABILITY IN THE AGENDA AND PROFESSIONAL LEGACY OF BRAZILIAN CFOS
summary: Objectives: To examine whether sustainability is central or peripheral in the agenda and legacy of Chief Financial Officers of large Brazilian firms, read against the attributes of responsible leadership. Theoretical framework: The study draws on responsible leadership theory, upper echelons theory and the institutional account of symbolic and substantive adoption known as decoupling. Method: A cross sectional survey of 106 CFOs of large Brazilian firms was analysed with descriptive statistics, comparing the prioritised ESG pillar, the weekly agenda for sustainability and technology, the professional legacy and the ethical self assessment. Results and discussion: Technology took more of the weekly agenda than sustainability, 21.1% against 15.2%. ESG was read as governance by 77.4%, against 16.0% environmental and 6.6% social, and sustainability figured in none of the legacies CFOs would leave. Ethics was rated high by 80.2% yet rested on conduct rather than structures. The finance apex enacts the individual attributes of responsible leadership and leaves the systemic ones symbolic. Research implications: Advancing the Sustainable Development Goals inside firms depends less on endorsement than on moving sustainability from a professed value to an operative priority and from governance towards the environmental and social dimensions. Originality and value: The study relocates the symbolic and substantive distinction from firm disclosure to the finance leader's stated agenda, with emerging economy evidence on a role the literature has overlooked.

title: Building Africa's Digital & AI Foundation: Data Infrastructure & Trust
summary: Building Africa's Digital Foundation: Data, Infrastructure and Trust is the inaugural whitepaper in a thought leadership series exploring the forces shaping Africa's digital and artificial intelligence future. Written from the perspective of a telecommunications and data transformation leader, the paper argues that Africa's next era of economic growth will be built on the strategic combination of digital infrastructure, data, and trust. Drawing on examples from Ghana and across the African continent, the paper examines how connectivity, cloud platforms, digital identity systems, fintech innovation, artificial intelligence, and modern data ecosystems are becoming the foundational layers of a new digital economy. Positioned at the intersection of technology, business strategy, and public policy, the paper presents a framework for policymakers, business executives, technology leaders, and development practitioners seeking to accelerate digital transformation while ensuring that growth remains inclusive, ethical, and economically meaningful. As the first publication in a broader series, Leading Africa's Digital & AI Future, it establishes the central thesis that Africa's digital future will be determined not only by the technologies it adopts, but by the institutions, governance structures, talent ecosystems, and trust frameworks it builds around them. Subsequent papers expand on these themes by examining the evolution from digital foundations to data intelligence, artificial intelligence, digital leadership, and the future of value creation in African organizations.

title: Digital Transformation and Low-Carbon Transition Risk in Manufacturing Firms: A Green Innovation Perspective
summary: Promoting the digital transformation of manufacturing and reducing the risks of the low-carbon transition are necessary steps to achieve carbon peaking and neutrality goals and drive all-round green development. Using publicly listed manufacturing enterprises in China from 2010 to 2024 as the research sample, this paper empirically examines the effect of digital transformation on corporate vulnerability to low-carbon transition and identifies the corresponding transmission paths. Digital transformation will reduce the risk of the low-carbon transition for manufacturing companies. Green innovation provides a necessary path for digital transformation to mitigate the aforementioned risk. After adding another category to the classification of innovation drivers, this study found that substantive green innovation significantly mediated the effect, but strategic green innovation did not. Therefore, digital transformation is likely to drive high-quality substantive changes rather than a large number of symbolic ones. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the risk-reducing effect of digital transformation is more pronounced in companies with a higher proportion of skilled technical staff, chair–CEO separation and those facing looser financing constraints. The above results provide empirical support and policy references for promoting the synchronous digital-green development of manufacturing enterprises and for identifying and mitigating low-carbon transition risks.

title: Entrepreneurship-Based Green Finance Model: Optimizing the Role of Regional-Owned Enterprises (BUMD) in Achieving Jakarta’s Net Zero Emission 2060 Target
summary: This study aims to examine and analyze the effects of willingness to innovate, proactive attitude, and risk-taking propensity on green finance and sustainability performance among Regional-Owned Enterprises (BUMD) in DKI Jakarta. The research employs a quantitative method using Structural Equation Modeling with Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) analysis, based on primary survey data collected from 23 BUMDs in Jakarta in 2025. The findings reveal that willingness to innovate and proactive attitude positively contribute to strengthening green finance; however, only the proactive attitude consistently enhances sustainability performance. Conversely, the willingness to take risks shows a negative effect on green finance and an insignificant impact on sustainability performance. Furthermore, green finance exerts a positive, though not yet significant, influence on sustainability performance. These findings underscore the need for operational strategies such as strengthening green innovation, establishing sustainability teams, implementing green risk management, and developing sustainability reports as integral components of transparent and accountable governance. Such strategies are essential to reinforce the strategic role of BUMDs in supporting the transition toward a green economy and achieving Jakarta’s Net Zero Emission 2060 target.

title: The Accountability Pathway: Linking ESG Disclosure, Integrated Reporting Quality, and Value Creation in Southeast Asia
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines how listed firms in Southeast Asia translate internal environmental, social, and governance (ESG) commitments into accountable practices, transparent reporting, and organizational value creation. Focusing on firms in the ASEAN‐6 countries over the period 2020–2024, the study proposes and empirically tests a framework in which ESG disclosure enhances integrated reporting quality and, ultimately, value creation, as measured by investment efficiency, while accounting for macro‐level energy transition pressures and firm‐level corporate governance mechanisms. Using panel data from 2605 firms, the study employs maximum likelihood structural equation modeling within a moderated mediation framework, while controlling for country‐level fixed effects. The findings indicate that ESG disclosure significantly enhances integrated reporting quality and that reporting quality serves as a key mechanism through which ESG disclosure contributes to value creation. The results further demonstrate that the accountability pathway is context‐dependent: energy transition pressures strengthen the importance of sustainability accountability, whereas corporate governance influences firms' capacity to implement ESG strategies effectively. This study contributes to the literature by conceptualizing corporate social responsibility as a multistage process that links ESG knowledge, disclosure and reporting infrastructure, and value creation. The findings offer practical implications for managers, investors, and policymakers seeking to enhance corporate transparency and promote sustainable capital allocation across ASEAN economies.

title: Blockchain Management Empowering Green and Climate Finance: Mechanisms, Real‑World Dilemmas and Optimization Paths
summary: Against the background of China's dual-carbon strategic goals, green and climate finance have achieved rapid scale expansion as critical instruments for low-carbon economic transition. Nevertheless, the whole market is still plagued by prominent governance risks, including intentional environmental data manipulation, and repeated double-counting of carbon assets, as well as poor traceability of green project capital flows. As an innovative trust-rebuilding management paradigm rather than simple technical tools, blockchain management leverages distributed ledgers, data immutability and smart-contract functions to deliver credible technical support for green-climate finance. This paper adopts qualitative analytical research, including literature review and dual-case comparison, to investigate how blockchain management functions within green credit, carbon trading and green bond scenarios. It identifies major practical obstacles and puts forward coordinated institutional-technical optimization proposals. The study reveals that blockchain can effectively mitigate information asymmetry in green-financial practice. Nevertheless, its large-scale commercial deployment is hindered by on-chain-off-chain data fragmentation, insufficient unified regulatory standards and relatively high technical operation costs. Therefore, collaborative governance mechanisms, unified industry-wide standards and lower access thresholds for small- and medium-sized enterprises are urgently required for future development.

title: ESG measurement, innovation pathways, and sustainable firm value creation: A systematic review of metrics, mechanisms, and contexts
summary: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance is increasingly linked to firm value through innovation, yet evidence remains fragmented across measurement systems, mechanisms, and contexts (Li & Sutunyarak, 2024; Widyantoro et al., 2025). This study systematically reviews how ESG is measured, which innovation pathways connect ESG to value creation, and which contextual conditions shape these relationships. Following PRISMA 2020, 60 Scopus- and Web of Science-indexed studies published between 2022 and 2026 were analyzed. The findings show that ESG ratings, composite scores, and disclosure-based indicators dominate measurement, while green innovation, technological innovation, digital transformation, research and development (R&D) intensity, and innovation capability constitute the main transmission pathways. Firm value is most frequently assessed through return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), Tobin’s Q, profitability, enterprise value, and broader performance indicators. Overall, ESG is associated with favorable firm-level outcomes, but these effects depend on credible measurement, active innovation mechanisms, and supportive organizational and institutional conditions. For industry, the findings support integrating ESG with innovation capabilities; for research and academia, they highlight the need for more comparable ESG measures and context-sensitive models of sustainable value creation.

title: Impacting Green Finance on Sustainable Agricultural Development: Evidence from Vietnam
summary: The transition toward sustainable agriculture requires substantial financial resources aligned with environmental and social objectives. Green finance has emerged as a critical instrument for mobilizing such resources; however, the mechanisms by which institutional, technological, and market forces shape green finance and translate into sustainable agricultural development remain underexplored, particularly in emerging economies. This study investigates the determinants of green finance and its role in promoting sustainable agricultural development in Vietnam. Using a mixed-methods approach, qualitative interviews with 45 experts in green farm economics and agrarian project financing were conducted first to develop context-specific measurement scales. Subsequently, a large-scale survey of 900 respondents from farm cooperatives, agricultural enterprises, green project participants, and green supply chain actors was conducted. The proposed research model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results reveal that environmental regulation pressure is the most influential driver of green finance, followed by stakeholder and market ESG pressure and digital financial inclusion. Green finance significantly promotes sustainable agricultural development and serves as a key transmission mechanism linking institutional, technological, and market factors to sustainability outcomes. Moreover, green supply chain requirements and ESG governance and transparency significantly strengthen the effectiveness of green finance and policy instruments. This study contributes to the literature by integrating green finance, ESG governance, and supply chain perspectives into a unified framework and provides important policy implications for promoting sustainable agriculture in emerging economies.

title: Sustainable accounting and its impact on business development: A systematic review
summary: This systematic literature review (SLR) examines how sustainable accounting influences business development by synthesizing evidence from 71 articles published between 2020 and 2025 and indexed in Scopus and Web of Science (WoS). The objective of this study was to analyze the influence of sustainable accounting on business development and identify the main organizational challenges, implementation strategies, and outcomes associated with its adoption. Using the PICO strategy and the PRISMA protocol, the study identifies key organizational challenges, implementation strategies, and outcomes related to sustainable accounting. The findings show that sustainable accounting strengthens business development through corporate social responsibility (CSR), sustainability reporting, environmental management accounting, technological innovation, risk management, cost efficiency, and long-term value creation. In particular, 42 percent of the reviewed studies emphasized improvements linked to social responsibility and corporate governance, while the remaining evidence highlighted financial transparency, technological innovation, and environmental accounting practices. Consistent with Schaltegger et al. (2022) and Alsarayrah et al. (2024), the review concludes that sustainable accounting is both a managerial and strategic tool for integrating economic, social, and environmental performance. The article contributes by systematizing recent evidence, identifying research gaps, and supporting the adoption of sustainable accounting practices for long-term business development.

title: ESG and Profitability in the Palm Oil Industry: A Literature Review
summary: Profitability is a key indicator of performance for oil palm plantation companies, but long-term profitability is increasingly influenced by their ability to manage environmental, social, and governance (ESG) risks and opportunities. This article presents a narrative literature review to develop an ESG-based sustainability model and examine its relationship with profitability, primarily proxied by Return on Assets (ROA). The Environmental dimension covers emissions reduction, biodiversity protection, land management, waste and water management, and sustainable production. The Social dimension encompasses worker welfare, occupational safety, community relations, human rights, and smallholder inclusion. The Governance dimension includes board oversight, transparency, risk management, compliance, and stakeholder accountability. The synthesis indicates that sustainability standards and early adoption can influence palm oil company performance, although financial impacts vary because ESG implementation involves costs alongside benefits such as operational efficiency, market access, reputation, and risk reduction. The proposed model positions ESG as a multidimensional strategic capability that influences profitability through operational efficiency, risk reduction, legitimacy, market access, and stakeholder trust. This article provides a conceptual foundation for future empirical testing of oil palm plantation companies without claiming statistical results from company data.

title: ASSESSMENT OF ESG REPORTING AMONG MONGOLIA’S TOP 100 COMPANIES
summary: Abstract Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting is an internationally standardized framework for assessing corporate sustainability, social responsibility, and long-term value creation. According to IBM, ESG represents an integrated framework for sustainability assessment. In Mongolia, formal regulation of ESG reporting was introduced in 2022 following the revision of the Regulation on Public Information Transparency by the Financial Regulatory Commission and the Mongolian Stock Exchange, which established mandatory disclosure requirements for ESG-related information for publicly listed companies. In parallel, the ESG Sustainability Reporting Guideline approved in 2022 has been undergoing alignment with the international IFRS S1 standard during 2024–2025. The objective of this study is to evaluate the current level of ESG disclosure among Mongolia’s TOP 100 companies as identified by the Mongolian National Chamber of Commerce and Industry in 2024. Of the TOP 100 companies, 25 firms that publicly disclosed ESG reports were selected for analysis. A total of 375 qualitative assessments were conducted across 15 indicators grouped into the three core ESG pillars—Environmental (E), Social (S), and Governance (G). Following qualitative scoring, company rankings and quantitative statistical analyses were performed using SPSS, including Ranking, One-way ANOVA, Welch and Brown–Forsythe robust tests, and post hoc comparisons. The One-way ANOVA results indicate no statistically significant differences in mean ESG scores across industry sectors (F(4,20)=0.98, p=.44). Levene’s test confirmed homogeneity of variances (p=.809), while the Welch (p=.65) and Brown–Forsythe (p=.49) robust tests similarly revealed no statistically significant inter-sectoral differences. Although the effect size (η²=.16) suggests a moderate practical effect, the absence of statistical significance may be attributable to the relatively small sample size and uneven distribution of firms across sectors. Post hoc analyses consistently grouped all sectors into a single homogeneous subset, further confirming the lack of statistically meaningful differences. The findings suggest that ESG reporting among Mongolia’s leading companies has not yet reached a level of sectoral differentiation, with systemic challenges related to data availability, reporting quality, and standard implementation remaining prevalent. Comparative analysis across ESG components shows that Environmental (E) disclosure scores highest, followed by Social (S) performance at a moderate level, while Governance (G) disclosure remains comparatively weak. As ESG reporting practices improve and data coverage expands, future research will enable more evidence-based assessments of sectoral policy implications, corporate governance quality, and social responsibility performance in Mongolia.

title: Investing with a conscience: the impact of ESG performance on corporate financing ease in Western Europe
summary: This study examines the impact of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance on corporate financing strategies in Western Europe, focusing on debt maturity and financing structure. Using a panel dataset of 8,592 firm-year observations from 706 listed non-financial firms during 2009–2021, the results show that stronger ESG performance is associated with longer debt maturity and greater reliance on internal financing. Mechanism analysis further indicates that improved ESG performance alleviates firms’ financing constraints, thereby reduce financing frictions. These findings suggest that strong ESG performance increases both shareholder and creditor confidence, enabling firms to secure more favorable financing conditions. Additional analysis reveals stronger effects among non-state-owned enterprises and firms with lower leverage. The findings remain robust across a battery of robustness and endogeneity tests and provide important implications for investors, corporate managers, and policymakers regarding the strategic role of ESG performance in corporate financing decisions and long-term sustainable development.
